title: Volozhin
hook: Rabbi Chaim of Volozhin founds a new kind of yeshiva

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Vilna Gaon: a scholar who lived inside his books and fought the new Hasidic movement. Your line was the genius of vilna. Whose learning did you stop to honor? Today, one of his students opens a door. Day nine hundred sixty-seven.

A long wooden table. Two young men bent over one open book, and both of them talking at once. One reads a line out loud, in a singsong. The other shakes his head: no, that can't be what it means, look at the next word. They argue, they laugh, they go back to the line. Down the table another pair is doing the same, and another, and another. The noise is more like a market than a library. Someone walking past the door might think a fight had broken out. It hasn't. This is what serious study sounds like here. Today we go into a study hall in a small town called Volozhin.
screen: `TWO YOUNG MEN, ONE BOOK.` → `BOTH TALKING AT ONCE.` → `A HALL THAT SOUNDS LIKE A MARKET.`

segments.voice: Rabbi Chaim of Volozhin had been a student of the Vilna Gaon, the scholar from yesterday. He took his teacher's love of study and gave it a building. Histories remember it as a new kind of academy: one that gathered students from many places, who left home to live and learn there, and that was supported by gifts from Jewish communities far beyond Volozhin itself. It belonged, in a sense, to everyone who paid for it. Tradition says the sound of learning in its hall was meant never to stop, day or night, with students taking turns. Why would that matter so much? Chaim wrote a book, Nefesh HaChaim, and in it he teaches that Torah study is not only good for the person studying. He describes it as something that helps hold the whole world in being. Seen that way, a hall where the learning never stops is not a school schedule. It is a kind of watch kept for the world. And notice how the learning happens: in pairs, out loud, arguing. The book of Proverbs has a line for it. In the King James wording: "Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend." The Talmud, in tractate Taanit, reads that verse about two students of Torah, who sharpen each other the way two blades do. And in the same passage a rabbi says he learned much from his teachers, more from his friends, and most of all from his own students. That is the idea of the yeshiva. You do not learn Torah alone and then bring it to others. You learn it across a table, from someone who refuses to let your first answer stand.
screen: `A STUDENT OF THE VILNA GAON.` · `STUDENTS GATHERED FROM MANY PLACES.` · `STUDY THAT HELPS HOLD THE WORLD.` · `IRON SHARPENS IRON.` · then, large: `LEARNED ACROSS A TABLE.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: study alongside others, even for a moment. Sit comfortably and let your breath settle. Bring to mind one person who has sharpened you: a friend who argued back, a coworker who asked the question you missed, a child who asked why. Picture the two of you at a table with something open between you. What did they show you that you couldn't see alone? Then think of one thing you'd like to understand better, and one person you might learn it with. Just hold the two of them together. The bell holds the time.
Yeshiva. An academy for the study of Torah and Talmud, where students often learn in pairs, out loud. Volozhin's gathered students from many places. Today's word.
Your line: the yeshiva. Today, learn one thing with someone else instead of alone. Ask a question and let them push back. Day nine hundred sixty-seven.

howItsDone: In yeshivas today, students commonly study Talmud in pairs called chavruta, reading aloud and debating each line, in a shared hall called the beit midrash.
